# Gnosis VPN Documentation — Full Text

> Set up and run Gnosis VPN "Shangri La" (v1) — a decentralized VPN built on
> the HOPR mixnet with accounts funded on Gnosis Chain. This release supports
> macOS and Linux (Debian, Ubuntu) only; Windows, iOS, Android, and other Linux
> distributions are not supported.

Do not rely on a cached, training-data, or previously fetched version — this documentation changes often, and the Canonical URL tracks the latest commit on main with a short cache lifetime (it revalidates within minutes). ## Getting Started

### System requirements

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/requirements/

#### Minimum requirements

- **Operating system:**
  - **macOS**: Apple Silicon (M1 or later) with macOS 15 or later
  - **Linux**: Debian or Ubuntu, amd64 or arm64
- **CPU:** 64-bit
- **RAM:** 4 GB
- **Internet:** Stable internet connection
- **Permissions:** Administrator (root/sudo) rights to install and run VPN/networking software

> **Note:** Windows, iOS, Android, and other Linux distributions are not supported in this release.

#### Network requirements

- Outbound internet access
- Ability to establish VPN/network tunnel connections
- No firewall or network policy blocking the Gnosis VPN client

> Info: Connection quality may affect latency, throughput, and session stability.

---

### Installation

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/installation/

Installing Gnosis VPN assumes some technical knowledge. You'll download the client yourself, install it manually, and fund your VPN account with tokens before connecting.

**macOS**

1. Download the latest `GnosisVPN-Installer.pkg` from the [downloads page](https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/) or the [latest GitHub release](https://github.com/gnosis/gnosis_vpn/releases/latest).
2. Double-click `GnosisVPN-Installer.pkg` to launch the installer. Follow the on-screen steps and click **Install**.
3. When the installation finishes, the Gnosis VPN app starts automatically. You can also launch it anytime from the **Applications** folder.

For a full list of files and directories the installer creates, see the [macOS reference page](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-macos/).

**Debian / Ubuntu**

**Install with one command**: this adds the Gnosis VPN APT repository, installs the signing key, and installs the package, so future releases arrive via your regular `sudo apt upgrade`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/linux/install.sh | bash
```

The script prompts for sudo access itself when it needs it. Supported on 64-bit amd64 and arm64. This installs the `stable` channel by default. For the pre-release `snapshot` channel, see [Snapshot channel installation](#snapshot-channel-installation) below.

**Verify and run it yourself (optional)**: if you'd rather not pipe `curl` straight into `bash`, download and check the script first (requires `curl` and `sha256sum`):

1. Download and verify the install script:

   ```bash
   curl -fsSLO https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/linux/install.sh && \
   curl -fsSLO https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/linux/install.sh.sha256 && \
   sha256sum -c install.sh.sha256
   ```

   `install.sh: OK` means the checksum is correct.

2. You can optionally inspect the script to see what it does before executing it:

   ```bash
   less install.sh
   ```

3. Then execute it (it will prompt for sudo access itself):

   ```bash
   bash install.sh
   ```

4. Launch the Gnosis VPN app from your application menu, or from the
   terminal:

   ```bash
   gnosis_vpn-app
   ```

#### Release channel installation

```bash
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings

sudo curl -fsSLo /etc/apt/keyrings/gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg \
  https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/linux/apt/gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg

sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gnosisvpn.sources > /dev/null <<'EOF'
Types: deb
URIs: https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/linux/apt
Suites: stable
Components: main
Architectures: amd64
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg
EOF

sudo apt update

sudo apt install gnosisvpn
```

Replace `amd64` with `arm64` if that's your machine's architecture.

#### Snapshot channel installation

This is experimental: `snapshot` tracks pre-release builds that haven't been promoted to `stable` yet.

```bash
sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings

sudo curl -fsSLo /etc/apt/keyrings/gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg \
  https://download.gnosisvpn.io/linux/apt/gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg

sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/gnosisvpn.sources > /dev/null <<'EOF'
Types: deb
URIs: https://download.gnosisvpn.io/linux/apt
Suites: snapshot
Components: snapshot
Architectures: amd64
Signed-By: /etc/apt/keyrings/gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg
EOF

sudo apt update

sudo apt install gnosisvpn
```

Replace `amd64` with `arm64` if that's your machine's architecture.

For a full list of files and directories the installer creates, see the [Debian reference page](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-debian/).


#### After installing

Your Gnosis VPN account must be funded before you can connect. See [Funding your account](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/funding/) for the next step.

---

### Funding your account

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/funding/

After installation, your Gnosis VPN account must be funded before you can connect. Gnosis VPN runs on Gnosis Chain and needs two tokens there: **wxHOPR**, which pays the nodes that carry your traffic, and **xDAI**, which pays network fees.

> Tip: Privacy consideration If you want stronger privacy, consider separating your everyday wallet from the one you use to fund your Gnosis VPN account. Because blockchain transactions are public, it's best to reduce onchain links between identities before acquiring HOPR. For example, you can use [privacypools.com](https://privacypools.com) to deposit ETH from your regular wallet into a pool on Ethereum mainnet, wait until your transaction blends with others, and then withdraw to a fresh wallet. To improve privacy, avoid withdrawing a unique amount. Choose a common denomination (e.g. 0.01 ETH) that many others are likely to use. You can then use the ETH in the new wallet to acquire HOPR and fund your Gnosis VPN account while keeping identities more separate. This makes it harder to link your everyday wallet to your Gnosis VPN usage, but it does not guarantee anonymity. Your privacy level depends on factors like pool size, timing, amount selection, and your overall onchain behavior.

#### Funding your account for the first time

When you first open the app, it shows **Fund your VPN** with two ways to fund:

- **Open funding site** opens the [funding site](https://funding.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/) with your VPN address filled in. Pay with a token you already hold, on Gnosis Chain, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Polygon, BNB Chain or Linea. The site converts it and delivers wxHOPR, plus a little xDAI for fees, to your VPN address.
- **Send funds directly** shows your VPN address as text and QR code, your current wxHOPR and xDAI balances, and how much of each to send at least. Send both tokens to that one address, on Gnosis Chain only: tokens sent on another network won't arrive.

Funds usually arrive within about 2 minutes. The app then finds your best route.

#### Topping up your account

1. Open the Gnosis VPN app and go to **Settings → Usage**.
2. Under **Funding**, choose **Open funding site** or **Add funds directly**. They work as described above.

The Usage tab also warns when xDAI for fees runs low.

#### Getting wxHOPR and xDAI yourself

Only needed if you send funds directly and don't hold these tokens yet.

##### Step 1: Buy HOPR and DAI

Buy HOPR and DAI on Ethereum Mainnet using:

- a centralized exchange (e.g. Coinbase), or
- a decentralized exchange such as [CowSwap](https://swap.cow.fi/).

##### Step 2: Bridge tokens to Gnosis Chain

You can bridge your tokens using one of the following options.

**Option A: Use the Gnosis Chain Bridge**

1. Go to the [Gnosis Chain Bridge](https://bridge.gnosischain.com/).
2. Connect your wallet on Ethereum Mainnet.
3. Select DAI and bridge it to Gnosis Chain. Once completed, you will have xDAI.
4. Stay on the Gnosis Chain Bridge.
5. Select HOPR and bridge it to Gnosis Chain. Once completed, you will have xHOPR.

**Option B: Use Trust Wallet**

1. Open Trust Wallet.
2. Use the built-in Swap / Bridge feature.
3. Bridge DAI → xDAI and HOPR → xHOPR. Trust Wallet will guide you through the process and handle the cross-chain transfer.

##### Step 3: Wrap xHOPR to wxHOPR

1. Open [https://wrapper.hoprnet.org/](https://wrapper.hoprnet.org/)
2. Connect your wallet on Gnosis Chain.
3. Convert xHOPR → wxHOPR.

#### Funding via the faucet

If you have been given a secret code, you can also fund your Gnosis VPN account via the faucet:

[https://faucet.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo](https://faucet.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo)

#### Your identity

Every Gnosis VPN node manages access to the tokens it needs to function via a Safe smart account powered by HOPR Safe Staking. Your identity key is what links your client to that Safe, which handles payment channels and ticket settlement on Gnosis Chain.

> Warning: Warning! If the identity file is deleted or lost, the client generates a new one, meaning any funds, open payment channels, or Safe association tied to the old identity are no longer reachable from that client and can't be restored.

Where your identity is stored:

Each user on the computer has their own identity, one per network. `<network>` is the network folder the client creates.

**macOS**

- Identity (`hopr.id` and `hopr.pass`): `~/Library/Application Support/GnosisVPN/networks/<network>/`
- Safe (`hopr.safe`): `~/Library/Caches/GnosisVPN/networks/<network>/`

**Debian / Ubuntu**

- Identity (`hopr.id` and `hopr.pass`): `~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/<network>/`
- Safe (`hopr.safe`): `~/.cache/gnosisvpn/networks/<network>/`


To use your account on another device, see [How do I move my identity to another device?](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/faq/#move-identity-to-another-device)

For a complete list of files and directories used by Gnosis VPN, see the reference pages for [macOS](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-macos/) and [Debian](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-debian/).

---

### Managing the client

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/managing-the-client/

Common lifecycle operations for the Gnosis VPN client: restarting the service, upgrading, and uninstalling.

#### Restarting the client service

**macOS**

In a terminal, run:

```bash
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
```

**Debian / Ubuntu**

In a terminal, run:

```bash
sudo systemctl restart gnosisvpn.service
```


#### Upgrading

**macOS**

To upgrade Gnosis VPN, download and run the latest installer, following the same steps as in the [installation guide](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/installation/). The installer will replace your existing version while preserving your configuration and identity. When upgrading from a release that kept one identity for the whole computer, the installer moves that identity to the user logged in at the screen. If nobody was logged in, see [My account is missing after upgrading from an earlier release](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/common-issues/#identity-not-migrated).

**Debian / Ubuntu**

In a terminal, run:

1. Refresh your system's package list so it knows about the latest Gnosis VPN release:

   ```bash
   sudo apt update
   ```

2. Upgrade Gnosis VPN:

   ```bash
   sudo apt upgrade gnosisvpn
   ```

When upgrading from a release that kept one identity for the whole computer, the upgrade moves that identity to the user logged in at the desktop. If nobody was logged in, see [My account is missing after upgrading from an earlier release](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/common-issues/#identity-not-migrated).


#### Uninstalling

**macOS**

In a terminal, run:

```bash
sudo /Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/uninstall.sh
```

**Debian / Ubuntu**

In a terminal, run:

```bash
sudo apt remove gnosisvpn
```


Uninstalling does not remove the identities stored in each user's home directory. See the file locations for [macOS](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-macos/) and [Debian](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-debian/).

## Advanced

### Using your own Blokli

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/advanced/custom-blokli/

Gnosis VPN reads everything it needs from Gnosis Chain, such as your Safe, your balances, your payment channels and the exit nodes registered on-chain, through **Blokli**, the HOPR on-chain indexer and GraphQL API. By default, the client uses the hosted Blokli for its network, `https://blokli.piz-palu.gnosisvpn.io` for `piz-palu-prod`.

You can run your own Blokli and point the client at it instead. The client then sends its on-chain queries to your Blokli and no longer depends on the hosted one.

If you run a Gnosis VPN exit node, its Blokli needs two extra settings. See [Run Blokli for an exit node](#run-blokli-for-an-exit-node).

#### Before you start

1. **Run Blokli and wait for its first sync.** Follow the HOPR guide [Run Blokli locally](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally) up to and including [Wait for the first sync](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#wait-for-the-first-sync). Skip its [Connect your node to Blokli](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#connect-your-node-to-blokli) section: it is for HOPRd nodes, and this page replaces it for Gnosis VPN.

2. **Index the network your client uses.** The current release runs on `piz-palu-prod`, the network the HOPR guide sets up. The client names your identity folder after the network Blokli reports, so a Blokli that indexes another network gives you a new, unfunded identity instead of your funded one.

3. **Check that Blokli is ready.** On the machine running Blokli, run:

   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:8080/readyz
   ```

   Continue when the response shows `"status":"ready"`. Until then, the client can't start and keeps retrying.

#### Choose your Blokli URL

The client needs Blokli's base URL, without `/graphql`:

| Where Blokli runs                          | Blokli URL                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| On the same computer as Gnosis VPN         | `http://localhost:8080`                                                     |
| On another machine in your network         | `http://<BLOKLI_IP>:8080`, where `<BLOKLI_IP>` is that machine's IP address |
| Behind your own HTTPS proxy or on a domain | `https://<your-blokli-domain>`                                              |

- If you [changed Blokli's port](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#change-the-default-ports), use that port instead of `8080`.
- If Blokli runs on another machine, allow its port in that machine's firewall. The connection is plain HTTP, so use it only on a network you trust.
- The host name must resolve to an IPv4 address. The client doesn't connect to Blokli over IPv6.

#### Point the client at your Blokli

The Blokli URL is a setting of the client service, so it applies to every user on the computer. Changing it restarts the service, which drops an active VPN connection.

**macOS**

The URL is set in the service definition, `/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist`.

1. Replace the URL, using your Blokli URL in place of `http://localhost:8080`:

   ```bash
   sudo plutil -replace EnvironmentVariables.GNOSISVPN_HOPR_BLOKLI_URL -string "http://localhost:8080" /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

2. Check the new value:

   ```bash
   plutil -extract EnvironmentVariables.GNOSISVPN_HOPR_BLOKLI_URL raw /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

3. Reload the service so it reads the changed file. A restart with `launchctl kickstart` keeps the old URL.

   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootout system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

   If `bootstrap` fails with `Input/output error`, the service hasn't finished stopping yet. Wait a few seconds and run it again.

> Caution: Installing a new version of Gnosis VPN replaces this file and sets the hosted Blokli again. Repeat these steps after every upgrade.

**Debian / Ubuntu**

The URL is set in `/etc/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn-dynamic.env`, which the package writes during installation. To change it, reinstall the package with your URL, using your Blokli URL in place of `http://localhost:8080`:

1. Refresh the package list:

   ```bash
   sudo apt update
   ```

2. Reinstall Gnosis VPN with your Blokli URL:

   ```bash
   sudo env GNOSISVPN_HOPR_BLOKLI_URL=http://localhost:8080 apt-get install --reinstall gnosisvpn
   ```

   The package checks the URL, writes it and starts the service again.

3. Check the new value:

   ```bash
   cat /etc/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn-dynamic.env
   ```

   The file should contain `GNOSISVPN_HOPR_BLOKLI_URL=` followed by your URL.

Upgrades with `apt upgrade` keep your URL. Re-running the [install script](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/installation/) with `--network` replaces it with the hosted Blokli of that network.


#### Check that the client uses your Blokli

Start the client from the app or with `gnosis_vpn-ctl`, then open your [worker log](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/logs/).

- A line with `blokli network` and `piz-palu-prod` means the client reached your Blokli and runs on the right network.
- `blokli network not queryable - retrying`, followed by your URL, means the client can't query your Blokli yet. Check that Blokli is running, that `/readyz` reports `ready`, and that the URL and port are right. The client keeps retrying, so it starts on its own once Blokli answers.

#### Switch back to the hosted Blokli

Repeat the steps in [Point the client at your Blokli](#point-the-client-at-your-blokli) with the hosted URL, `https://blokli.piz-palu.gnosisvpn.io`.

On macOS, installing Gnosis VPN again also restores it.

#### Run Blokli for an exit node

Exit nodes are paid through PIX payments, which settle through the Curvy contracts on Gnosis Chain. Blokli indexes these contracts only when you turn this on, so a Blokli for an exit node needs two extra settings.

Follow the HOPR guide [Run Blokli locally](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally), with these changes:

1. **Turn on Curvy indexing before the first start.** After the guide's [Set up Blokli](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#set-up-blokli) steps, and before you start Blokli, open `docker-compose.yml` in the `docker` folder of the Blokli repository. Under the `bloklid` service, add two lines to its `environment` section and keep the line already there:

   ```yaml title="docker-compose.yml" {4-5}
   bloklid:
     environment:
       RUST_LOG: info,blokli_chain_indexer=debug
       BLOKLI_CURVY_AGGREGATOR: "0x3f2B578C6844b8D65b67dba4107db61D51b9020C"
       BLOKLI_INDEXER_ENABLE_CURVY_INDEXING: "true"
   ```

   - `BLOKLI_CURVY_AGGREGATOR` is the Curvy Aggregator contract. Blokli finds the other Curvy contracts from it when it starts.
   - `BLOKLI_INDEXER_ENABLE_CURVY_INDEXING` makes Blokli index the Curvy notes and nullifiers that PIX payments create, along with the HOPR data.

2. **Start Blokli and check the setting.** Continue with the guide's [Start Blokli](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#start-blokli) and [Wait for the first sync](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#wait-for-the-first-sync). In the configuration Blokli prints at startup, next to `network: piz-palu-prod`, check for:

   ```text
   indexer.enable_curvy_indexing: true
   ```

3. **Connect your exit node.** Your exit node runs HOPRd, so follow the guide's [Connect your node to Blokli](https://docs.hoprnet.org/node/run-blokli-locally#connect-your-node-to-blokli) to set its `blokli_url`. With the DAppNode exit node package, enter the URL in the setup wizard's **Blokli provider URL (advanced)** field instead.

> Caution: Blokli can't add Curvy indexing to data it has already indexed without it. If you add the settings to a Blokli that has synced before, it refuses to index, and its log shows `Missing address/topic info in log topic info table`. To fix this, delete the indexed data and sync again from the start. This repeats the whole first sync. ```bash docker compose down -v ``` ```bash docker compose up -d ```

---

## Concepts

### What is Gnosis VPN?

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/introduction/overview/

Gnosis VPN is a privacy-focused VPN built on the HOPR mixnet. It lets you route internet traffic through HOPR-based infrastructure instead of sending it through a single centralized VPN provider. The aim is to provide a familiar VPN experience while reducing the amount of metadata exposed to any single party.

#### How it differs from a traditional VPN

Traditional VPNs usually create an encrypted tunnel between you and one VPN provider. This can hide your IP address from websites, but it also means the VPN provider may be able to observe connection metadata.

Gnosis VPN takes a different approach by using HOPR as the routing layer underneath the VPN client. This reduces reliance on a single trusted operator and is designed to limit what can be observed about your activity, including where traffic comes from, where it exits, and when communication happens.

---

### Shangri La v1

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/introduction/shangri-la-v1/

The current release of Gnosis VPN is **Shangri La**, version 1.0. It runs a decentralized VPN architecture on the HOPR mixnet and replaces all earlier releases.

#### What Shangri La supports

- A functional VPN client
- HOPR-based routing
- End-to-end encrypted tunnelling
- Exit nodes discovered at runtime, with multiple locations
- On-chain metered payments
- macOS
- Linux (Debian, Ubuntu)

#### What Shangri La does not support yet

> Info: Shangri La does not yet support Windows, Linux distributions other than Debian and Ubuntu, or mobile.

#### Earlier releases

Releases up to 0.97.1 run on networks that shut down on **21 November 2026**, and stop working then. Upgrade to Shangri La before that date, as described in [Managing the client](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/managing-the-client/).

---

### Architecture overview

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/introduction/architecture/

Gnosis VPN is a decentralized VPN built on top of the HOPR mixnet, designed to provide privacy-preserving internet access without relying on centralized infrastructure.

Unlike a traditional VPN, where traffic usually goes through servers controlled by one company, Gnosis VPN uses a decentralized network of independent nodes. This helps reduce reliance on a single provider and improves privacy.

Gnosis VPN is composed of several main components:

- **Client**: the user-facing application or CLI and local components such as Root and Worker.
- **The HOPR network**: provides the decentralized routing layer.
- **Exits**: exit nodes, which run the Gnosis VPN server side and forward VPN traffic to the public internet.

![Gnosis VPN architecture: the Client (App UI/CLI, Root System Service, Worker Process) connects through the HOPR network to the Exit nodes.](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/img/gnosis_vpn_architecture.png)

#### Client

The client runs on your device and is responsible for managing the VPN connection. It includes the user-facing application or CLI, as well as local components that prepare and maintain the connection. The client offers three binaries:

- `gnosis_vpn-root`
- `gnosis_vpn-worker`
- `gnosis_vpn-ctl` (CLI)

The client system service (`gnosis_vpn-root`) runs with root privileges and takes care of routing setup. It spawns the worker process (`gnosis_vpn-worker`), which is responsible for the application logic and runs as the user who started the client. The control application (`gnosis_vpn-ctl`) is used to manage the client and its connections.

#### The HOPR network

Gnosis VPN routes traffic through the HOPR mixnet, a decentralized network designed to protect both data and metadata. Instead of a single tunnel, traffic is relayed across multiple independent nodes, making it difficult to trace user activity or correlate network patterns. Gnosis VPN is implemented as a service layer on top of this network, rather than replacing it.

#### Exits

Exit nodes are the server-side endpoints of a Gnosis VPN connection. They receive the VPN connection from the client side and forward your traffic to the public internet. In the Gnosis VPN architecture, an exit node runs the Gnosis VPN server component together with a WireGuard server.

During connection setup, the client-side Worker communicates with the selected exit node, registers the client's WireGuard public key, and opens the required network sessions. After that, the local VPN interface can be brought up on your device.

An exit node is responsible for:

- Accepting the client connection
- Registering the client's WireGuard public key
- Managing the WireGuard server-side configuration
- Forwarding VPN traffic to the public internet
- Returning responses back to the client through the VPN path

The visible IP address and location are determined by the exit node's network connection. For example, if the selected exit node is hosted in a specific region, websites will usually see traffic as coming from that region.

> Info: Exit nodes should not be described as ordinary HOPR relay nodes. In this context, they are Gnosis VPN server-side nodes that use the HOPR-based connection flow and provide the final path from the VPN tunnel to the public internet.

Their availability and performance may depend on several factors, including server uptime, public reachability, network configuration, WireGuard configuration, and the selected route through the network.

---

### How does Gnosis VPN work?

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/introduction/how-it-works/

Gnosis VPN operates by replacing the traditional, centralized VPN model with a decentralized, multi-hop routing system. Instead of trusting a single company's server with your traffic, Gnosis VPN separates the connection process across three distinct layers: your local client, the decentralized HOPR network, and an independent exit node.

#### Establishing a connection

1. **Connection initiation and local setup.** When you start a connection via the app or CLI (`gnosis_vpn-ctl`), your device's root system service (`gnosis_vpn-root`) takes charge. To keep your system secure, it spawns an unprivileged worker process (`gnosis_vpn-worker`) that handles the actual application logic and network communication. The worker runs as the user who requested the connection.

2. **Secure handshake via the mixnet.** Instead of connecting directly to a VPN server, the worker process routes its initial communication through the HOPR mixnet. It uses this decentralized network of independent nodes to securely reach your selected exit node. Over this secure HOPR path, the worker registers your client's WireGuard public key and opens the necessary TCP and UDP sessions.

3. **Establishing the WireGuard tunnel.** Once the exit node accepts the connection and registers your key, the worker signals the root service to bring up the local VPN interface. Simultaneously, the exit node configures its side of the connection. This establishes a secure WireGuard tunnel between your device and the exit node, with the HOPR network acting as the transport layer in between.

#### The traffic flow

Once the connection is fully established, your internet traffic follows a unique, privacy-preserving path:

- **From your device:** data enters the local WireGuard tunnel.
- **Through the HOPR network:** the data is relayed across multiple independent nodes in the HOPR mixnet. This multi-hop process protects your metadata, making it difficult for anyone to trace your activity or correlate network patterns.
- **To the exit node:** the traffic arrives at the exit node (the Gnosis VPN server), which acts as the bridge between the HOPR network and the regular web.
- **To the public internet:** the exit node forwards your traffic to its final destination. Websites will see the IP address and geographical location of the exit node, not your actual device.

When websites respond, the data travels back through the exit node, back across the HOPR mixnet, and finally to your device. By never relying on a single trusted intermediary, this architecture keeps your browsing activity private.

---

## FAQ & troubleshooting

### Common issues

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/common-issues/

Find the problem that matches your symptoms and open it for the fix.


#### Connected, but no internet (or unstable)

The VPN reports a connected state, but internet access is missing or drops in and out.

**Symptoms**

- The client status shows "Connected", but web browsers display timeout errors.
- Internet routing functions intermittently or drops completely every few minutes.
- IP verification websites (e.g. `ifconfig.me`, `icanhazip.com`) fail to load.

**Resolution steps: macOS and Linux with GUI**

1. **Switch exit nodes:** click the location dropdown and select an alternative node with the lowest available latency (ms).
2. **Verify your balance:** open **Settings → Usage**. Ensure your balance is sufficient; top up if it is depleted, as described in [Funding your account](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/funding/#topping-up-your-account).
3. **Hard restart:** completely terminate the application. Right-click the Gnosis VPN tray icon, select **Quit**, and relaunch the application.

**Resolution steps: Linux without GUI**

1. Check your node and wallet status by verifying your Safe and channel balances with your active exit node:
   ```
   gnosis_vpn-ctl balance
   ```
2. If your balance is sufficient, restart the background service to flush stuck routing tables:

   ```
   # Linux
   sudo systemctl restart gnosisvpn.service

   # macOS
   sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
   ```


#### Connecting takes over a minute or never completes

The client hangs indefinitely in a "Connecting" state when attempting to establish a tunnel with an exit node.

**Symptoms**

- The interface or terminal status stays frozen in the connecting phase for over 1–2 minutes.
- Specific geographic locations fail to hand over traffic, while others connect instantly.
- Connection eventually succeeds, but only after an unacceptable delay.

**Resolution steps: macOS and Linux with GUI**

1. Open **Settings → Usage** to verify your balance.
2. Pick an alternate exit node with lower latency.
3. Restart the app via the tray icon menu if it remains frozen.

**Resolution steps: Linux without GUI**

1. Inspect the handshake state:
   ```
   gnosis_vpn-ctl status
   ```
2. Force a reconnection to a different node endpoint:
   ```
   gnosis_vpn-ctl connect --node <alternative_node_id>
   ```


#### The app looks blurry or the wrong size when display scaling is enabled (Linux)

The Gnosis VPN app is built on GTK3, which runs through the legacy X11 compatibility layer on Wayland. This can cause incorrect scaling when display scaling is set manually.

**Resolution steps**

Find the scaling option for legacy (X11) apps in your desktop environment's display settings and set it to **"Scaled by the system"**.

On KDE, this is typically found under **Display Configuration**:

![KDE legacy X11 app scaling setting](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1fa3e541-dbb8-45aa-bad8-7877d57a9a93)


#### A thin transparent line appears below the title bar on Linux

On some Linux desktops, a 1-pixel fully transparent line can appear just below the window's title bar. It's easiest to notice when another window is directly behind Gnosis VPN, since whatever is behind shows through that single pixel row.

This happens because the app window doesn't set a custom title bar, so it uses your desktop's native GTK client-side decorations (CSD). GTK CSD windows get rounded corners and a drop shadow drawn by the compositor as an alpha-blended mask around the window. That mask's edge sits right at the boundary between the GTK-drawn title bar and the embedded WebKitGTK content area, and its antialiasing doesn't line up exactly with where the webview starts painting, leaving a single device pixel row with no opaque paint, so the compositor blends in whatever is behind the window.

This is a known class of rendering artifact with GTK CSD + WebKitGTK (and shows up in other Linux apps built the same way, including Electron/Chromium apps with rounded CSD corners). It's purely cosmetic and does not affect the VPN connection or app functionality.

**Resolution steps**

No action required. This is a cosmetic rendering artifact only. It doesn't affect the VPN connection or app functionality, and can be safely ignored.


#### Gnosis VPN doesn't start after an update

The client fails to start after an update and shows **Critical error during initialization**. This happens when you have used an earlier release of Gnosis VPN: the latest release runs on a different network, but your machine still holds the identity created on the old one. The safe belonging to that identity does not exist on the new network, so startup fails and retries in a loop.

**Symptoms**

- The app shows **Critical error during initialization**, with a construction or chain error mentioning the network endpoint.
- Syncing appears to resume on its own, then the same error returns shortly after.
- The service log repeats the same failure every 10 seconds:
  ```
  INFO  hopr_lib::builder: registering safe with this node safe_addr=<safe_address>
  ERROR hopr_lib::builder: safe registration failed safe_addr=<safe_address> error=safe registration error: safe <safe_address> does not exist
  WARN  hopr_chain_connector::connector: chain subscription stream ended, marking chain health as degraded
  ERROR gnosis_vpn_lib::hopr::api: error=Construction error: chain error: safe registration error: safe <safe_address> does not exist
  ERROR gnosis_vpn_lib::core: hopr runner failed to start - trying again in 10 seconds
  ```

**Resolution steps**

Resetting the client means moving your identity aside, which keeps it as a backup, and letting the client generate a new one on the current network. `<name>` is your account name on this computer and `<network>` is the network folder the client created.

> Warning: These steps set aside the identity the client is currently using. The renamed `<network>.reset-<timestamp>` folder is your backup: confirm it exists before starting the service again. The backup is what lets support restore your previous identity if it is ever needed.

**macOS**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootout system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
   ```
2. Move your identity aside. This renames `networks/<network>` to `networks/<network>.reset-<timestamp>` in both your identity and safe folders, and moves any identity left over from a previous release aside as well:
   ```bash
   sudo gnosis_vpn-migrate start-clean --user <name>
   ```
3. Confirm the backup exists before continuing. The list should show `<network>.reset-<timestamp>` and no `<network>` folder:
   ```bash
   ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/
   ```
   If `<network>` is still listed, rename it yourself, in both folders:
   ```bash
   mv ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/<network> ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/<network>.reset-<timestamp>
   ```
   ```bash
   mv ~/Library/Caches/GnosisVPN/networks/<network> ~/Library/Caches/GnosisVPN/networks/<network>.reset-<timestamp>
   ```
4. Start the service again:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

**Debian / Ubuntu**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl stop gnosisvpn.service
   ```
2. Move your identity aside. This renames `networks/<network>` to `networks/<network>.reset-<timestamp>` in both your identity and safe folders, and moves any identity left over from a previous release aside as well:
   ```bash
   sudo gnosis_vpn-migrate start-clean --user <name>
   ```
3. Confirm the backup exists before continuing. The list should show `<network>.reset-<timestamp>` and no `<network>` folder:
   ```bash
   ls -la ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/
   ```
   If `<network>` is still listed, rename it yourself, in both folders:
   ```bash
   mv ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/<network> ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/<network>.reset-<timestamp>
   ```
   ```bash
   mv ~/.cache/gnosisvpn/networks/<network> ~/.cache/gnosisvpn/networks/<network>.reset-<timestamp>
   ```
4. Start the service again:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl start gnosisvpn.service
   ```


The client generates a new identity on the current network at the next start. This is a fresh account, so you need to fund it before you can connect. See [Funding your account](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/funding/).


#### My account is missing after upgrading from an earlier release

Earlier releases kept one identity for the whole computer. On upgrade, the installer moves it to the user logged in at the screen (on Linux the desktop session, on macOS the console user). If nobody was logged in, the move is deferred: the previous identity stays in its old location, locked to root.

**Symptoms**

- After the upgrade, the client shows a new, unfunded account instead of your previous one.
- The app shows **Gnosis VPN service is not running** and lists `gnosis_vpn-migrate` commands instead of a Start button.
- The installer output says `Migrate it later with: sudo gnosis_vpn-migrate identity --user <name> --replace`.

**Resolution steps**

`<name>` is the account on this computer that should own the previous identity. `--replace` moves any identity that account already has to `networks/<network>.replaced-<timestamp>`, so nothing is deleted. Without it, the command stops with exit code 75 when the account already has a different identity.

**macOS**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootout system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
   ```
2. Move the previous identity to your account:
   ```bash
   sudo gnosis_vpn-migrate identity --user <name> --replace
   ```
3. Start the service again. The first command re-enables it in case the installer left it disabled:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl enable system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
   ```
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

The migration log is `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/migrate.log`.

**Debian / Ubuntu**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl stop gnosisvpn.service
   ```
2. Move the previous identity to your account:
   ```bash
   sudo gnosis_vpn-migrate identity --user <name> --replace
   ```
3. Enable and start the service again, in case the installer left it disabled:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl enable --now gnosisvpn
   ```

The migration log is `/var/log/gnosisvpn/migrate.log`.



#### The VPN is in use by another user

Only one user at a time can run the VPN on a computer. While another user has the client running, you can't start or control it.

**Symptoms**

- The app shows **The VPN is in use by another user on this computer**.
- `gnosis_vpn-ctl` prints `Worker client is in use by another user of this machine - wait until they stop it`.
- `gnosis_vpn-ctl ping` and `gnosis_vpn-ctl info` still work.

**Resolution steps**

Wait until the other user stops the client, then start it from your own account. Start it as yourself, not with `sudo`: the client always runs as the user who starts it, and root can't own it.

To start it from a terminal, `<keep-alive>` is how long the client keeps running without receiving a command:

```bash
gnosis_vpn-ctl start-client <keep-alive>
```


#### Connecting fails with “refusing to connect without DNS diversion”

The client could not point your system's DNS at the tunnel. It refuses to connect instead of sending your DNS queries outside the VPN.

**Symptoms**

- Connecting fails right after the tunnel is set up, for every exit node.
- The service log has an error line `refusing to connect without DNS diversion`, followed by `DNS not diverted:` and the reason each method failed.

**Resolution steps: Linux**

1. Find the reason in the service log. The error line only summarizes each failure; the warnings just before it carry the system error:
   ```bash
   sudo grep -B 10 "refusing to connect without DNS diversion" /var/log/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn.log | tail -n 11
   ```
2. If those warnings mention `Read-only file system`, a drop-in may have narrowed the service's writable paths. The service needs `/etc` and `/run/resolvconf` writable. Check with:
   ```bash
   systemctl show gnosisvpn -p ReadWritePaths
   ```
   If either is missing, find the drop-in that sets `ReadWritePaths`, `ReadOnlyPaths` or `ProtectSystem` with `systemctl cat gnosisvpn`, remove that setting or the whole drop-in, then reload and restart:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl daemon-reload
   sudo systemctl restart gnosisvpn
   ```
3. If `/etc/resolv.conf` is managed by a tool other than systemd-resolved, resolvconf or NetworkManager, report it as described below, with the log attached.


#### Still not working?

If the steps above don't resolve it, attach your client logs to your support ticket. See [Finding your logs](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/logs/) and [Reporting issues](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reporting/reporting-issues/).

---

### Frequently asked questions

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/faq/

Open a question to see the answer.


#### How do I move my identity to another device?

Your identity links the client to your Safe and the funds in it. A new device creates its own identity, which is a new, unfunded account. To keep using your account, copy your identity folder from the old device to the new one.

The folder is named after the network. For the current release that is `piz-palu-prod`:

- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/GnosisVPN/networks/piz-palu-prod/`
- Debian / Ubuntu: `~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/piz-palu-prod/`

Copy the whole folder, not just the files in it. Other folders next to it, such as `piz-palu-prod.reset-<timestamp>`, are older identities set aside. You don't need them. The two devices can run different operating systems.

> Warning: Anyone with a copy of this folder can use your account and its funds. Keep the copy private. Use your identity on one device at a time: after the move, don't start the client on the old device again.

`<backup>` below is where you keep the copy, such as a USB drive. Run the commands as the user who runs Gnosis VPN. Only the service commands need `sudo`.

**On the old device**

**macOS**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootout system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
   ```
2. Copy your identity folder to `<backup>`:
   ```bash
   cp -R ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/piz-palu-prod <backup>/
   ```

**Debian / Ubuntu**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl stop gnosisvpn.service
   ```
2. Copy your identity folder to `<backup>`:
   ```bash
   cp -R ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/piz-palu-prod <backup>/
   ```


**On the new device**

Install Gnosis VPN first, as described in the [installation guide](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/get-started/installation/). If the app shows a new account, don't fund it: your copied identity replaces it. Then:

**macOS**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootout system/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient
   ```
2. Move aside the identity the new device created, and its safe folder. This keeps them as a backup. If `mv` reports `No such file or directory`, there is nothing to move:
   ```bash
   mv ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/piz-palu-prod ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/piz-palu-prod.replaced-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
   ```
   ```bash
   mv ~/Library/Caches/GnosisVPN/networks/piz-palu-prod ~/Library/Caches/GnosisVPN/networks/piz-palu-prod.replaced-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
   ```
   The safe folder holds the Safe of the new identity. With it moved aside, the client looks up the Safe of your copied identity on-chain.
3. Copy your identity folder into place and make it private to your account:
   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks
   ```
   ```bash
   cp -R <backup>/piz-palu-prod ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN/networks/
   ```
   ```bash
   chmod -R go-rwx ~/Library/Application\ Support/GnosisVPN
   ```
4. Start the service again:
   ```bash
   sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist
   ```

**Debian / Ubuntu**

1. Stop the service:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl stop gnosisvpn.service
   ```
2. Move aside the identity the new device created, and its safe folder. This keeps them as a backup. If `mv` reports `No such file or directory`, there is nothing to move:
   ```bash
   mv ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/piz-palu-prod ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/piz-palu-prod.replaced-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
   ```
   ```bash
   mv ~/.cache/gnosisvpn/networks/piz-palu-prod ~/.cache/gnosisvpn/networks/piz-palu-prod.replaced-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
   ```
   The safe folder holds the Safe of the new identity. With it moved aside, the client looks up the Safe of your copied identity on-chain.
3. Copy your identity folder into place and make it private to your account:
   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks
   ```
   ```bash
   cp -R <backup>/piz-palu-prod ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/
   ```
   ```bash
   chmod -R go-rwx ~/.local/share/gnosisvpn
   ```
4. Start the service again:
   ```bash
   sudo systemctl start gnosisvpn.service
   ```


Open the app and check **Settings → Usage**. It should show your account's balance, not a new, empty account.

---

### Log location

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/logs/

#### Gnosis VPN app

If you are using the Gnosis VPN desktop app, logs can be exported directly from the application:

1. Open the Gnosis VPN app.
2. Click the **Settings** button with the gear icon.
3. In the **Troubleshooting** section, click **Export logs…**.
4. Attach the exported log file when reporting the issue.

The export is one compressed file with system information, the app logs, the service log and the worker logs. Worker logs are only included when you are the user running the client.

#### Terminal

The service runs as root and writes to a system log. The worker runs as the user who started the client and writes to that user's home directory.

##### macOS

If you are using Gnosis VPN on macOS without exporting logs from the desktop app, log files can be found in:

| Path                                                                     | Content                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/gnosisvpn.log`                                  | Service log.                                   |
| `~/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/worker.log.YYYY-MM-DD`                         | Worker log, one file per day, the last 7 kept. |
| `~/Library/Logs/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/gnosis_vpn-app.<date>.log` | App log.                                       |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/updates.log`                                    | Updater log.                                   |

###### Installer logs

If the issue occurred during installation, the macOS installer writes separate logs:

| Path                                                | Content                        |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/installer.log`   | Main installer log.            |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/preinstall.log`  | Preinstall script output.      |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/postinstall.log` | Postinstall script output.     |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/migrate.log`     | Identity migration on upgrade. |

##### Linux

If you are running Gnosis VPN on Linux without the desktop app, log files can be found in:

| Path                                                                     | Content                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `/var/log/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn.log`                                       | Service log.                                   |
| `~/.local/state/gnosisvpn/worker.log.YYYY-MM-DD`                         | Worker log, one file per day, the last 7 kept. |
| `~/.local/state/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/gnosis_vpn-app.<date>.log` | App log.                                       |
| `/var/log/gnosisvpn/migrate.log`                                         | Identity migration on upgrade.                 |

## Reporting

### Reporting issues

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reporting/reporting-issues/

Bug reports should include enough information to understand what happened, when it happened, and how to reproduce it. Before opening a new report, check whether the issue has already been reported.

#### Where to report

Use GitHub Discussions first for user reports, questions, and reproducible issues.

- [Gnosis VPN GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/gnosis/gnosis_vpn/discussions)
- [Category: Issues & Bug Reports](https://github.com/gnosis/gnosis_vpn/discussions/categories/issues-bug-reports)

If the issue is confirmed or requires developer tracking, it may later be moved or linked to a GitHub Issue.

Official support channels may also be used if provided during onboarding, for example:

- Telegram → [@GnosisVPN_Support](https://t.me/GnosisVPN_Support)
- Signal → `GnosisVPN_Support.01`
- Email → `support@gnosisvpn.com`

Use the support channel that was provided to you during testing or onboarding.

#### What logs to include

Include logs from the affected environment.

**Export logs from the Gnosis VPN app:**

1. Open the Gnosis VPN app.
2. Click the **Settings** button with the gear icon.
3. In the **Troubleshooting** section, click **Export logs…**.
4. Attach the exported log file when reporting the issue.

The export contains system information, the app logs, the service log and the worker logs. Worker logs are only included when you are the user running the client.

**Or find the log files based on your environment:**

| Log                | macOS                                            | Linux                                            |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Service            | `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/gnosisvpn.log`          | `/var/log/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn.log`               |
| Worker             | `~/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/worker.log.YYYY-MM-DD` | `~/.local/state/gnosisvpn/worker.log.YYYY-MM-DD` |
| App                | `~/Library/Logs/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/`  | `~/.local/state/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/`  |
| Identity migration | `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/migrate.log`  | `/var/log/gnosisvpn/migrate.log`                 |
| Updater            | `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/updates.log`            | —                                                |
| Installer          | `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/`             | —                                                |

See [Finding your logs](https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/troubleshooting/logs/) for details.

**Uploading log files:**

Instead of attaching the exported (compressed) log file to your report, you can upload it via the log uploader and reference it:

[https://log-uploader.gnosisvpn.com/](https://log-uploader.gnosisvpn.com/)

#### How to describe reproduction steps

When reporting an issue, describe the steps as clearly and simply as possible. The report should explain what action was performed, what was expected to happen, what actually happened, and whether the issue is reproducible.

##### Title

Use a short, clear title that starts with `[Bug]:`. Examples:

- `[Bug]: Connected, but websites do not load`
- `[Bug]: Connection takes more than 2 minutes`
- `[Bug]: App reconnects repeatedly after connecting`
- `[Bug]: Selected location is not available`

##### Issue description

Describe the problem in a clear and simple way. Include:

- What you were trying to do
- What happened instead
- Whether the issue happened once or repeatedly
- Any visible error messages or unusual app behavior
- Screenshots or screen recordings, if useful

> Example: I connected to the Netherlands – Amsterdam exit location. The app showed "Connected", but websites did not load. The issue happened several times after reconnecting.

##### Steps to reproduce

List the exact steps needed to reproduce the issue.

**Example (GUI):**

1. Open the Gnosis VPN app.
2. Select Netherlands – Amsterdam as the exit location.
3. Click Connect.
4. Wait until the app shows Connected.
5. Open a website in the browser.

**Example (CLI / without GUI):**

1. Start the Gnosis VPN service.
2. Connect to an exit location using the CLI.
3. Run `gnosis_vpn-ctl status`.
4. Check internet access in the browser or another application.

##### Environment / versions

Include information about your system and Gnosis VPN version:

- Operating system
- Gnosis VPN package version
- Installation type: desktop app / CLI / headless
- Exit node
- Approximate time of the issue

> Example: OS: Ubuntu 24.04 · Package version: x.xx.x · Installation type: desktop app · Exit location: Netherlands – Amsterdam · Time: 2026-05-21 12:40

##### Acknowledgement

Before submitting the report, confirm that you have searched for existing issues and discussions. In the GitHub form, check **"I have searched for existing issues and discussions."**

A clear report with logs, version information, and reproduction steps makes it easier to understand and resolve the issue.

## Reference

### File locations on macOS

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-macos/

This page lists every file and directory the macOS installer creates, for users who want to audit the installation or locate specific files.

#### Directories created by the installer

| Folder                                    | Purpose                   | Owner        | Permissions | Notes                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------------ | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/Library/Application Support/GnosisVPN/` | Service working directory | `root:wheel` | `0755`      | Helper scripts, `installer/` network choice, updater state                       |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/`                | Service log directory     | `root:wheel` | `0755`      | `gnosisvpn.log` (service log) and `updates.log` (updater); rotated via newsyslog |
| `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/installer/`      | Installer log directory   | `root:wheel` | `0755`      | `installer.log`, `preinstall.log`, `postinstall.log`, `migrate.log`              |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/`                         | Configuration directory   | `root:wheel` | `0755`      | Network configs and the `config.toml` symlink                                    |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/templates/`               | Network config templates  | `root:wheel` | `0755`      | One `<network>.toml.template` per shipped network                                |

- After an upgrade from a single-user release, `/Library/Application Support/GnosisVPN/` keeps the previous identity as `.config.migrated-<timestamp>` (or `.config.<timestamp>.bak` after a reset), `root` `0700`.
- `/etc` is a symlink to `/private/etc` on macOS.

#### Key files placed into existing system directories

| Path                                                         | Purpose                             | Notes                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/usr/local/bin/gnosis_vpn-root`                             | Main VPN daemon binary              | `root:wheel`, `0750`                                            |
| `/usr/local/bin/gnosis_vpn-worker`                           | Worker process binary               | `root:wheel`, `0755`                                            |
| `/usr/local/bin/gnosis_vpn-ctl`                              | CLI control tool                    | `root:wheel`, `0755`                                            |
| `/usr/local/bin/gnosis_vpn-update`                           | Updater                             | `root:wheel`, `0755`                                            |
| `/usr/local/bin/gnosis_vpn-migrate`                          | Identity migration tool             | `root:wheel`, `0755`; migrates and resets identities            |
| `/usr/local/bin/gnosis_vpn-manager`                          | Management utility script           | `root:wheel`, `0755`                                            |
| `/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient.plist` | LaunchDaemon service definition     | Loaded and enabled at boot, runs as root                        |
| `/etc/newsyslog.d/gnosisvpn.conf`                            | Log rotation policy                 | `gnosisvpn.log` at 1 GB, 12 rotations                           |
| `/etc/sudoers.d/gnosis-vpn`                                  | Sudoers drop-in for service control | Passwordless service control for the `gnosisvpn` group; `0440`  |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/config.toml`                                 | Symlink to active network config    | Points to `<network>.toml` for the network chosen at install    |
| `/Applications/Gnosis VPN.app`                               | GUI application bundle              | Extracted from archive during postinstall; `root:admin`, `0755` |
| `/var/run/gnosisvpn.sock`                                    | Control socket                      | Created by the daemon at startup                                |
| `/var/run/gnosisvpn.pid`                                     | Daemon PID file                     | Written by the daemon at startup                                |
| `/var/run/gnosisvpn/`                                        | Runtime directory                   | `daemon.lock` and `teardown-state.json`                         |

- The sudoers drop-in lets the `gnosisvpn` group run specific `launchctl` and `gnosis_vpn-update` commands without a password. The installer adds the console user to the group.

#### Per-user files

The worker runs as the user who starts the client, so each user has their own identity, one per network. `<network>` is the network folder the client creates.

| Path                                                           | Content                                             | Permissions                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `~/Library/Application Support/GnosisVPN/networks/<network>/`  | Identity: `hopr.id` and `hopr.pass`                 | Directories `0700`, files `0600` |
| `~/Library/Caches/GnosisVPN/networks/<network>/`               | Safe: `hopr.safe`                                   | Directories `0700`, files `0600` |
| `~/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN/`                                    | Worker log `worker.log.YYYY-MM-DD`, the last 7 kept | `0700`                           |
| `~/Library/Application Support/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/` | App settings, `settings.json`                       |                                  |
| `~/Library/Logs/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/`                | App logs, `gnosis_vpn-app.<date>.log`               |                                  |

#### Uninstalling

The uninstall script removes the binaries, the launchd plists, `/etc/gnosisvpn` (backed up to `~/gnosis-vpn-config-backup-<timestamp>` first), `/Library/Logs/GnosisVPN`, the sudoers file, the `gnosisvpn` group and the app bundle.

It keeps `/Library/Application Support/GnosisVPN` and every user's files under `~/Library`.

---

### File locations on Debian / Ubuntu

Source: https://docs.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/docs/reference/file-locations-debian/

This page lists every file and directory the Debian package creates, for users who want to audit the installation or locate specific files.

#### Directories created by the installer

| Folder                      | Purpose                   | Owner       | Permissions    | Notes                                                                      |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------- | -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/`           | Configuration directory   | `root:root` | `0755`         | Env files, network configs, `version.txt` and the `config.toml` symlink    |
| `/var/lib/gnosisvpn/`       | Service working directory | `root:root` | `0755`         | Holds no identity, see the notes below                                     |
| `/var/log/gnosisvpn/`       | Log directory             | `root:root` | `0755`         | `gnosisvpn.log` (service log) and `migrate.log` (identity migration)       |
| `/run/gnosisvpn/`           | Runtime directory         | `root:root` | `0755`         | Created by systemd: `gnosisvpn.sock`, `daemon.lock`, `teardown-state.json` |
| `/etc/apt/keyrings/`        | APT signing keys          | `root:root` | `0644` (file)  | `gnosisvpn-archive-keyring.gpg`, copied during postinstall                 |
| `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/`  | APT repository source     | `root:root` | `0644` (file)  | `gnosisvpn.sources`, written during postinstall                            |
| `/usr/share/gnosisvpn/`     | Shared package resources  | `root:root` | `0644` (files) | The APT keyring and the `networks` list                                    |
| `/usr/share/doc/gnosisvpn/` | Documentation             | `root:root` | `0644` (files) | Copyright and changelog; removed on uninstall                              |

- The `config-*.toml` files in `/etc/gnosisvpn/` are `root:root` `0644`.
- After an upgrade from a single-user release, `/var/lib/gnosisvpn/` keeps the previous identity as `.config.migrated-<timestamp>` (or `.config.<timestamp>.bak` after a reset), `root` `0700`.
- The APT channel comes from `/etc/gnosisvpn/version.txt`. `stable` uses both mirrors, `https://download.vpn.gnosis.eth.limo/linux/apt` and `https://download.gnosisvpn.io/linux/apt`. `snapshot` and `experimental` use only `https://download.gnosisvpn.io/linux/apt`.

#### Key files placed into existing system directories

| Path                                                | Purpose                          | Notes                                                               |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/usr/lib/systemd/system/gnosisvpn.service`         | Systemd unit                     | Runs `gnosis_vpn-root` as `root`; enabled at install                |
| `/usr/lib/systemd/system/gnosisvpn-logrotate.timer` | Log rotation timer               | Checks the service log size every minute                            |
| `/etc/logrotate.d/gnosisvpn`                        | Log rotation policy              | Rotates `gnosisvpn.log` hourly or at 1 GB, keeps 12, gzip           |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/config.toml`                        | Symlink to active network config | Points to `config-<network>.toml` for the network chosen at install |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn.env`                      | Service environment variables    | `RUST_LOG=info`, logs to `gnosisvpn.log`, static routing forced     |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/gnosisvpn-dynamic.env`              | Generated environment overrides  | Network endpoint; overrides `gnosisvpn.env`, `0644`                 |
| `/etc/gnosisvpn/version.txt`                        | Installed version                | Picks the APT channel during postinstall                            |
| `/usr/share/gnosisvpn/networks`                     | Networks the package ships       | Space-separated, first is the default; replaced on upgrade          |
| `/etc/sysctl.d/99-gnosisvpn-bbr.conf`               | TCP congestion control           | Enables BBR and `fq` system-wide                                    |
| `/var/lib/dpkg/info/gnosisvpn.*`                    | dpkg package records             | dpkg's installed-file list and maintainer scripts                   |
| `/usr/bin/gnosis_vpn-migrate`                       | Identity migration tool          | `root:root`; migrates and resets identities                         |
| `/usr/bin/gnosis_vpn-update`                        | Updater                          | `root:root`                                                         |

- `gnosisvpn-dynamic.env` is written during postinstall. It takes precedence over `gnosisvpn.env`, which is left untouched so upgrades don't prompt.
- `/var/lib/dpkg/info/gnosisvpn.*` is created by dpkg, not by the package. dpkg runs these maintainer scripts on install, upgrade and removal.

#### Per-user files

The worker runs as the user who starts the client, so each user has their own identity, one per network. `<network>` is the network folder the client creates.

| Path                                            | Content                                             | Permissions                      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `~/.local/share/gnosisvpn/networks/<network>/`  | Identity: `hopr.id` and `hopr.pass`                 | Directories `0700`, files `0600` |
| `~/.cache/gnosisvpn/networks/<network>/`        | Safe: `hopr.safe`                                   | Directories `0700`, files `0600` |
| `~/.local/state/gnosisvpn/`                     | Worker log `worker.log.YYYY-MM-DD`, the last 7 kept | `0700`                           |
| `~/.config/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/`      | App settings, `settings.json`                       |                                  |
| `~/.local/state/com.gnosisvpn.gnosisvpnclient/` | App logs, `gnosis_vpn-app.<date>.log`               |                                  |

The service can only write under `/home` and `/var/home`. A home directory elsewhere is not supported.

#### Files changed while connected

Where systemd-resolved does not manage DNS, the service points the system resolver at the tunnel while connected. For this it can also write to `/etc` and `/run/resolvconf`.

| Path                                | Content                                                | Notes                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/etc/resolv.conf`                  | Nameservers replaced by the tunnel's; other lines kept | Only when neither systemd-resolved nor resolvconf manages it                                                                                                                      |
| `/etc/resolv.conf.gnosisvpn-backup` | The original `/etc/resolv.conf`                        | Restored and removed on disconnect, or at the next start after a crash. If restoring fails, it stays and the service log warns `cannot restore resolv.conf`; copy it back by hand |
| `/run/resolvconf/`                  | The tunnel's nameservers, registered with resolvconf   | Only when resolvconf manages `/etc/resolv.conf`; removed on disconnect                                                                                                            |

#### Removing and purging

- `apt remove` keeps `/etc/gnosisvpn`, `/var/lib/gnosisvpn` and `/var/log/gnosisvpn`.
- `apt purge` deletes `/etc/gnosisvpn` and `/var/log/gnosisvpn`, and moves any previous identity (`/var/lib/gnosisvpn/.config*`) to `/var/backups/gnosisvpn/<timestamp>/`, `root` `0700`. `/var/lib/gnosisvpn` itself is removed only if nothing else is left in it.
- Neither touches the per-user files above.
